output.title: Maintenance windows are a workflow decision, not a calendar slot
output.body:
If you run a 1–10-person business, rethinking maintenance windows is usually not a big strategy exercise. It is one recurring workflow decision: do you bundle changes into planned downtime, spread them through rolling updates, or use a hybrid?

The practical question is simple: which costs you more in your business, planned customer-visible downtime or unplanned breakdowns? That is the decision worth writing down before you touch any tooling.

Automation can help if the work is repeatable. For example, if you already use a standard pre-maintenance message, a checklist, a rollback step, and a log of what changed, then a small workflow can be designed around sequencing, reminders, and record-keeping. But the go/no-go call should stay with you. Human approval belongs at the point where service might be interrupted or risk increases.

If the process is mostly email, notes, and tool-jumping, the next step is not to automate first. Map the handoffs. Name the owner. Write the one outcome that matters. Then decide whether the window is really a candidate for AI assistance or just a manual habit with better labels.

That is the sort of boundary Bareni looks for in a diagnostic: one recurring workflow, one decision owner, one clear outcome. Some maintenance setups are a fit for a small pilot; others are better left manual. The useful part is finding the line before you build around the wrong one.
